abstract: Background: Negative affect and low positive affect are linked to craving and relapse in methamphetamine use disorder (MUD). Brief positive autobiographical memory recall improves mood in non-clinical samples, but it has not been tested in people in treatment for MUD. We tested whether positive memory recall improves affective state, withdrawal and craving compared with a neutral recall condition. Methods: Adults with past-year MUD in their first year of abstinence were recruited from two residential treatment programs in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Participants were randomized, blinded to condition, to recall personally meaningful positive memories (Positive; n = 37) or emotionally neutral procedural memories (Procedural; n = 36) during a laboratory session. Positive and negative affect (PANAS, the prespecified primary outcomes), withdrawal (AWQ), craving (visual digital scale; Stimulant Craving Questionnaire), and anhedonia (SHAPS) were assessed before and approximately one hour after the recall. Group x Time effects were tested with mixed ANCOVAs adjusted for sex and age, with Holm and false discovery rate correction. Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were estimated for each outcome. Results: Of 80 randomized participants, 73 began the session and were analyzed. The Group x Time interaction was not significant for positive affect (p = .689) or negative affect (p = .399). Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were small and imprecise (positive affect: -0.53 points, 95% CI -2.60 to 1.53; negative affect: 0.54 points, 95% CI -0.90 to 1.99). Across both groups, negative affect, withdrawal, craving and desire to use decreased over the session, while positive affect also declined (all p [≤] .015). No secondary or exploratory outcome differed between conditions. Conclusions: A single positive autobiographical memory recall did not produce a detectable end-of-session difference in affect, withdrawal or craving relative to neutral recall in individuals with MUD. Affective and craving states shifted across the session regardless of memory content. Future work should test repeated or more intensive positive-affect interventions in this population.
